member: Dr. Elena Vasquez — Contact Dynamics and Slip Detection
message:
Slip needs two different signals, so steady grip and fast slip vibration must be separated. Plain words: the fingertip holds with steady shear force but warns from fast skin vibration, because vibration appears at micro-slip before the object visibly moves. The 2014 Wettels Chapter.pdf (E31) states Pacinian corpuscles respond 60 to 500 hertz and detect slip vibration as small as 1 micrometer at 200 hertz center frequency, and that BioTac slip power resides in 100 to 500 hertz separable from slower contact events, which is why Dr. Amara Okafor ridges feed this band and Prof. Kenji Tanaka must supply shear plus vibration for the slip warning concept (C15).

Timing decides whether the warning is useful, and fast sampling with a short window wins. Plain words: sample the vibration fast and decide within a blink so grip can tighten before gross slide. The 2014 Wettels Chapter.pdf (E31) samples the alternating current, Alternating Current means the fast vibration part, pressure signal at 2200 hertz and decides in 30 millisecond total window as half the 60 to 80 millisecond human grip reflex time; the stick-to-slip simulation (E38) shows micro-slip at 53.6 milliseconds and gross slip at 96.8 milliseconds with stick ratio falling 0.95 to 0.48, so a 30 millisecond detector fits inside the 43.2 millisecond gap for Dr. Marcus Reid to act.

High frequency sensing must use a different material from static force, and thin skin matters. Plain words: a piezoelectric film hears slip while capacitive taxels feel steady push, where piezoelectric means vibration makes voltage directly. The Revolutionizing Robot Touch with Advanced Tactile Sensors (E30) reports a 28 micrometer polyvinylidene fluoride film, Polyvinylidene Fluoride means PVDF piezoelectric plastic, gave a clear voltage jump as a bottle slipped, and 0.4 centimeter skin gave 2.2 to 2.6 volt slip signals versus 1.2 to 1.7 volt on 0.8 centimeter skin because thick silicone absorbs vibration; a 0.4 millimeter ridge pitch at 50 millimeter per second slip gives 125 hertz inside the 100 to 500 hertz band, which corrects the unit slip in the ridge-frequency calculation (E39). That is everyday scale: 200 hertz is a low electrical hum, 1 micrometer is about one-fiftieth of a hair width, and 30 milliseconds is about one-tenth of an eye blink.

Not ready, because Prof. Kenji Tanaka shear resolution and Dr. Marcus Reid 2200 hertz readout latency still must prove the 30 millisecond loop closes on hardware as a bench test.
